name: pe.ayni.architecture.ModularityTest
comment:
Verifies that the modules stay independent of one another.

This is the only architecture test in the project, and it is worth its three lines: it fails the build when a module reaches into another module's internals instead of going through its events or the interface it publishes. Without it, the boundaries are an agreement that erodes on the first hurried pull request.

methods.name: verifiesModularStructure
methods.comment: Fails when a module depends on the internals of another one.

methods.name: writesDocumentation
methods.comment:
Writes module diagrams under {@code target/spring-modulith-docs}.

They are generated from the code, so they cannot drift from what was actually built, which makes them good evidence for the architecture chapter of the report.

name: pe.ayni.booking.AdjustAvailabilityAcceptanceTest
comment:
US20 and US22 over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL: a tutor who pauses or changes one date sees the hours that already existed follow at once, one test per scenario of {@code features/US20-date-exceptions.feature} and {@code features/US22-pause-availability.feature}.

The tutor of {@link BookingScenario} is free tomorrow from nine to twelve, Lima time, with the hours already generated, which is exactly the case a pause usually meets: it arrives after the hours it covers exist. Matching is the real one, so the search is checked too.

methods.name: offersAt
methods.comment: Offers the search holds for the tutor's hour, read as rows: matching is another module.

name: pe.ayni.booking.AvailabilityTimesDatabaseTest
comment:
A tutor's wall clock times against a real PostgreSQL, written from a JVM that is not in UTC.

A {@code time} column holds a time of day with no zone, so 18:00 has to arrive as 18:00 from any machine. It did not: with {@code hibernate.jdbc.time_zone} set to UTC, Hibernate converted it through {@code java.sql.Time} in the JVM's zone and then wrote it in UTC. From a laptop in Lima, 18:00 to 21:00 reached the table as 23:00 to 02:00 and its CHECK refused the row, while the same request from docker compose, which runs in UTC, went through. Reading shifted the times back in the same JVM, so nothing looked wrong until two machines shared a database.

Configured like {@code TutorAvailabilityAcceptanceTest} so both share one Spring context, which is the only reason identity and skills are mocked here.

methods.name: aJvmInLima
methods.comment: Five hours behind UTC, like the laptops the team runs the backend on from the IDE.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookABlockAcceptanceTest
comment: US03 over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL, one test per scenario of {@code features/US03-book-a-block.feature}, plus the refusals the hold endpoint owes an honest answer.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingConfirmationDatabaseTest
comment: The two promises of the confirmation that only a real database can check: two transactions racing for one hour are decided by the version column, and a confirmation that fails after everything was written leaves nothing behind.

methods.name: theVersionColumnDecidesARaceAtConfirmation
methods.comment:
Scenario 4 at the worst possible moment, staged step by step rather than left to luck.

Ana's confirmation has already read the hour, with its version, and checked that her hold is alive; it is paused inside the charge, before touching anything. Meanwhile her hold runs out, Bruno takes the hour over and books it, and commits. When Ana's confirmation carries on, its update of the hour finds a version that is no longer there: it loses, and the charge it had just made rolls back with it.

methods.name: aFailureAfterEverythingWasWrittenLeavesNothingBehind
methods.comment:
Scenario 6 against the database: the confirmation fails just before committing, when the charge, the hours and the booking have all been flushed. The transaction rolls back whole, and the hold is given back in a second one.

Catching the failure inside the confirmation's transaction would have ended in {@code UnexpectedRollbackException}. It must not appear anywhere.

methods.name: walletsRefusalIsNotAnUnexpectedRollback
methods.comment: Wallet's refusal marks the confirmation's transaction for rollback. Because nobody catches it inside, the student gets the refusal itself, with the missing credits, and not an unexpected rollback.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingPersistenceTest
comment: {@code booking.bookings} against the PostgreSQL that has to keep its promises: the entity maps to the table Flyway created, the repository only answers within a university, and the constraints refuse what the entity would never build.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingScenario
comment:
The world every US03 scenario starts from, against a real PostgreSQL: a tutor of UPC who is free tomorrow from nine to twelve, Lima time, and two students, Ana and Bruno.

The tutor's hours are real: they are generated by declaring the availability over HTTP, the way US19 does it. identity and skills are the seams, mocked with the answers the real modules give. Wallet, sessions and everything inside booking are the real thing.

Every scenario class extends this one, so they all share one application context: the same mocks, the same clock, the same connection pool.

methods.comment: Tomorrow at that hour, Lima time, as the instant the API speaks in.

methods.name: grant
methods.comment: Credits that never expire, which is all most scenarios care about.

methods.name: chargesOf
methods.comment: Ledger entries that charged this student for a booking. The ledger is append only.

methods.name: sessionsOf
methods.comment: Sessions scheduled for this student, read as rows: sessions is another module.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingTestConfig
comment: What the booking scenarios add to the application: a clock they can move, and a way to make a confirmation fail at its very last moment.

methods.name: mutableClock
methods.comment: Replaces the system clock everywhere, wallet included, so every module agrees on now.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingTestConfig$FailingConfirmation
comment:
Makes the confirmation of a chosen student fail just before its transaction commits.

That is the worst moment to fail: the credits are charged, the hours are marked and the booking is saved, all of it flushed to the database. Scenario 6 has to show that even then the balance ends as it was and the hours end free.

methods.name: failNextConfirmationOf
methods.comment: The next confirmation of this student fails.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingTestDatabase
comment: The PostgreSQL booking's integration tests run against: one container for the whole run.

name: pe.ayni.booking.HoldRaceTest
comment: Several students choosing the same free hour at the same instant, each on a connection of their own. Whoever reads the hour after the winner committed is refused by the block; whoever read it free alongside the winner loses on the version column. Either way exactly one of them holds it.

name: pe.ayni.booking.HourBlockQueriesTest
comment: The hour block queries US03 relies on, against PostgreSQL: the stretch a student asks for comes back in one query and only from their university, the expired holds are found for the sweep, and the version column really makes a stale write lose. Also the hours {@link BookingApi#openHoursOf} hands to matching.

name: pe.ayni.booking.MutableClock
comment:
A clock a test can move: five minutes later, the hold has run out.

Every view of it taken with {@link #withZone} reads the same instant, so a use case asking for the university's local date and another asking for the instant agree on what now is. Shared between threads, which the concurrency tests need.

name: pe.ayni.booking.TutorAvailabilityAcceptanceTest

US19 over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL: declaring a weekly window is what makes its hours exist. One test per scenario of {@code features/US19-tutor-availability.feature} that booking can answer on its own.

identity and skills are the seams: their published interfaces are mocked with the answers the real modules give.

methods.name: tomorrowsWeekday
methods.comment: Tomorrow's weekday: it occurs exactly four times in the four weeks ahead, all in the future.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.BookHoursUseCaseTest

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.ConfirmBookingTest

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.DeclareWeeklyAvailabilityUseCaseTest
comment: A tutor cannot be free twice over the same hour.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.GenerateHourBlocksUseCaseTest

Generating the same horizon twice must not offer the same hour twice.

It happens for real: a tutor changing anything regenerates their availability, and a scheduled job walks the same days again the following night.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.ExpiredHoldsJobTest

US38 over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL: asking for a link, opening it, and every way opening it must fail. One test per confirmation scenario of {@code features/US38-request-access.feature}.

The people are the demo ones, created by {@link DemoIdentityData} itself, so the test signs in as the same Ana a developer signs in as. The raw token is read from {@link AccessRequested}, the way notifications will read it to send the email: the database only has its hash.

name: pe.ayni.identity.IdentityTestConfig

name: pe.ayni.identity.MutableClock
comment:
A clock a test can move: ten minutes later, the access link has expired.

The same idea as booking's, kept here because a module's tests do not reach into another module's test package.

name: pe.ayni.identity.application.ConfirmAccessUseCaseTest
comment: US38's confirmation without Spring: what it reads, what it refuses and what it writes.

name: pe.ayni.matching.MatchingTestDatabase

name: pe.ayni.matching.OfferProjectionListenersTest
comment:
Every event matching listens to, and what it leaves in {@code matching.available_offers}.

Each event is published inside a transaction, as its module publishes it, and heard once that transaction commits. Each one is also heard twice, because a retried event must neither duplicate an offer nor fail on one that is already there.

The four modules matching asks are mocked with the answers the real ones give. The table is read as rows, so what is checked is what the search will read.

name: pe.ayni.matching.SearchOffersAcceptanceTest
comment:
US01 over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL, one test per scenario of {@code features/US01-search-offers.feature}, plus the refusals the endpoint owes an honest answer.

The projection is filled the way it is in the application: booking's {@code HoursGenerated} is published and matching hears it. Skills, identity and reputation are the seams, mocked with the answers the real modules give. Every test searches a course of its own, so no test sees another one's offers.

methods.name: tomorrowAt
methods.comment: Tomorrow at that hour, Lima time, as the instant the API speaks in.

methods.name: tutorFreeAt
methods.comment: A tutor of the course, with that average, whose hours booking just generated.

methods.name: searchTomorrowAfternoon
methods.comment: Tomorrow afternoon, from two to six, Lima time.

name: pe.ayni.matching.SearchOffersEndToEndTest
comment:
US01 from end to end, the way a tutor and a student use it, with nothing written into the projection by hand.

The tutor offers a course through skills and declares availability through booking; the student finds the hours, holds them and books them. Skills, booking, wallet, reputation and matching are the real modules, talking through their events. Only identity is mocked, with the answers the real module gives, because the academic record it would read does not exist here.

The listeners run once the publisher's transaction commits and before the request answers, so each search sees what the previous request caused, the same way {@code BookABlockAcceptanceTest} sees the session its booking created.

methods.name: declareTomorrowMorning
methods.comment: Free tomorrow from nine to twelve, Lima time, every week.

methods.name: anaSearchesTomorrow
methods.comment: What Ana finds for the course tomorrow, all day.

comment: US01's search without Spring: what it asks the projection, and what it makes of the answer.

comment: US01, scenario 2: no tutor free in the window, so the closest hours outside it come back.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.AccessLinkEmailAcceptanceTest
comment:
US38 from the student's side: the link is asked for, arrives in the inbox, and opens a session.

Nothing is mocked. The email goes over SMTP to GreenMail, an SMTP server inside the test, and the test reads the link from the message the way the student would, then confirms it. Identity, notifications and the database are the real ones; the people are the demo ones, created by {@link DemoIdentityData} itself.

methods.name: theEmail

name: pe.ayni.notifications.NotificationsTestDatabase

US54 from the participants' side: the code arrives in each inbox and confirms presence.

Nothing is mocked. Sessions issues the codes through the use case its job calls, notifications emails them over SMTP to GreenMail, and the test reads each code from the email the way the participant would, then types it in. The people are the demo ones, Ana and Bruno, created by {@link DemoIdentityData} itself.

comment:
US02's standing endpoint over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL, one test per endpoint scenario of {@code features/US02-tutor-standing.feature}.

Skills is the seam, mocked with the answer the real module gives: whether the tutor may teach the course. Every test uses a tutor and a course of its own.

name: pe.ayni.reputation.application.TutorStandingQueryTest
comment: US02's standing lookup without Spring: a tutor with history, a new one, and a stranger.

name: pe.ayni.reputation.domain.TutorStandingTest

name: pe.ayni.sessions.CloseSessionAcceptanceTest
comment:
US11 over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL, one test per scenario of {@code features/US11-close-session.feature}, with scenario 3 of US54 as the unverified outcome.

Sessions are scheduled with the use case booking's event calls, joined and ended over HTTP, and their presence proved with the codes read from {@link PresenceCodeIssued}. The overdue ones are closed by calling the use case the job calls. Wallet is the real one, so each test also shows the money: the tutor paid, or the student refunded. Booking only answers the course.

methods.name: aSessionUnderway
methods.comment: A session ten minutes into its hour, joined by both, its codes sent, and the student charged one credit for it as booking would.

methods.name: endedAgo
methods.comment: Moves the session back so its booked hour ended that long ago.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.CloseSessionAcceptanceTest$Outcomes
comment: What sessions announced: the codes it sent, and how each session ended.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.JoinSessionAcceptanceTest
comment:
US08 over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL, one test per scenario of {@code features/US08-join-session.feature}.

Sessions are created the real way, by publishing the booking's {@code BookingConfirmed}. Booking is the seam, mocked with the answer the real module gives for the need description. Times are relative to now, so each test places its session where it needs it: about to start, too far ahead, or already over.

methods.name: aSessionStartingIn
methods.comment: A confirmed booking starting that long from now, which schedules its session.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.JoinSessionAcceptanceTest$StartedSessions
comment: Counts SessionStarted per session, from whichever thread published it.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.PresenceCheckAcceptanceTest
comment:
US54 over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL, one test per scenario of {@code features/US54-presence-code.feature}.

Sessions are scheduled with the use case booking's event calls, and joined over HTTP. The codes are issued by calling the use case the job calls, instead of waiting a minute for the job, and read from {@link PresenceCodeIssued}, the only place the code travels in clear besides the email. The email itself is covered by notifications' own acceptance test; here identity only answers who the participants are.

methods.name: aSessionStarting
methods.comment: A session scheduled to start that long ago (or from now, if positive), lasting one hour.

methods.name: aSessionTenMinutesIn
methods.comment: A session ten minutes into its hour, joined by both participants: its codes are due.

methods.name: anotherCode
methods.comment: A six digit code that is not this one.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.PresenceCheckAcceptanceTest$IssuedCodes
comment: The codes in clear, per session and participant, as notifications receives them.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.SessionOnBookingConfirmedTest
comment:
A confirmed booking creates its session, as the backend guide says sessions must.

The event is published inside a transaction, as booking publishes it: the listener runs once that transaction commits, and never when it rolls back.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.SessionsApiDatabaseTest
comment:
{@link SessionsApi} against PostgreSQL, the way recognition will call it.

Sessions are created the real way, by a confirmed booking. Nothing moves a session to COMPLETED yet (that arrives with US11), so the tests that need one mark it with SQL, as the story will once it closes sessions.

methods.name: aConfirmedBooking
methods.comment: A booking of that many hours, confirmed, which schedules its session. Returns the session.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.SessionsTestDatabase
comment: The PostgreSQL sessions' integration tests run against: one container for the whole run.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.SessionsServiceTest
comment: What sessions tells the other modules, without Spring.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.domain.PresenceCheckTest
comment: US54 without Spring: a code expires, counts wrong attempts, and is dead after five.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.domain.SessionTest
comment: A session is born scheduled, in a room of its own, and only its two participants get in.

name: pe.ayni.skills.CatalogSearchDatabaseTest
comment:
{@code GET /api/v1/catalog} over HTTP against a real PostgreSQL: the filters are optional parameters of one query, and whether PostgreSQL accepts them as {@code null} is only known by running it.

Every test works inside a category of its own, so rows left by other tests do not count.

name: pe.ayni.skills.OfferApprovedCourseAcceptanceTest
comment:
US13, over HTTP, against a real database.

One test per scenario of {@code src/test/resources/features/US13-offer-approved-course.feature}, with the same names, so that the acceptance criteria and what actually runs cannot drift apart quietly.

{@code identity} is mocked here on purpose: identity has no implementation yet, so this is the seam where skills is stubbed against the contract it depends on ({@link pe.ayni.identity.IdentityApi}), exactly the way the real one will answer once it exists.

methods.name: uniqueSuffix
methods.comment: A short suffix, unique per test run, that keeps course codes within their 32-character column.

methods.name: theUniversityAsksForThirteen
methods.comment: Background: the university's minimum teaching grade is 13.00, for every scenario.

name: pe.ayni.skills.OpenApiRequestHeadersTest
comment:
What Swagger UI is told about the {@code X-Tenant-Id} and {@code X-User-Id} headers.

It lives next to the other tests that share {@link SkillsTestDatabase}, because that is the database the application context starts against.

name: pe.ayni.skills.SkillsApiDatabaseTest
comment:
{@link SkillsApi} against a real PostgreSQL.

The unit tests of {@code SkillsService} mock the repository, so they cannot tell whether a query runs at all. This one exists because one did not: a derived query that promised identifiers and returned entities passed every mocked test and failed on the first real call.

Configured like {@code OfferApprovedCourseAcceptanceTest} so both share one Spring context.

name: pe.ayni.skills.SkillsTestDatabase
comment:
The PostgreSQL the integration tests run against.

A real one, and the same version {@code docker compose} uses, because the tests that need a database are about what the database itself does: the constraints that keep a global item from carrying a tenant and the unique index that refuses a tutor offering the same item twice. Neither exists in an in-memory database, and a test of a rule that is not there proves nothing.

One container for the whole test run. Starting it costs a couple of seconds; starting one per test class would cost that every time.

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.DeclareInterestsUseCaseTest
comment:
US40: registering what a student needs help with, and enabling what they can already teach, during the initial configuration.

{@link OfferApprovedCourseUseCase} is built for real here rather than mocked, wired to mocked repositories and identity underneath: mocking a concrete class needs bytecode instrumentation that some JDKs (this one included) refuse to perform, and asserting through the real object is the more faithful test anyway.

methods.name: approvedFor
methods.comment: Wires the mocks so offering {@code item} for {@code grade} succeeds through the real use case.

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.OfferApprovedCourseUseCaseTest
comment: US13: offering a university course the tutor's academic record already clears.

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.SkillsServiceTest
comment: What the rest of the platform is allowed to know about a tutor's skills.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.OfferedSkillTest
comment: US13: a course a tutor already passed is enabled the moment the grade clears the threshold.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.SkillsFixtures

methods.name: globalItem
methods.comment: A global tool: same for every university, no course code.

methods.name: universityItem
methods.comment: A course that belongs to {@link #UPC}.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.WalletBalanceAcceptanceTest
comment:
US23, over HTTP, against a real database.

One test per scenario of {@code src/test/resources/features/US23-wallet-balance.feature}, with the same names, so that the acceptance criteria and what actually runs cannot drift apart quietly.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.WalletEventListenersTest
comment:
What wallet does when something happens in another module.

The events are published inside a transaction, as the module that owns them would: the listeners run once it commits, so a session that is rolled back never credits anybody. Publishing them outside one would silently do nothing, which is worth knowing before writing a listener of your own.

methods.name: publish
methods.comment: Publishes as the owning module would: inside a transaction that then commits.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.WalletLedgerTest
comment:
The promises the ledger makes, checked against the database that has to keep them.

None of these can be tested anywhere else: the trigger belongs to PostgreSQL, the agreement between the balance and the history is about rows that were really written, the chain of hashes only proves anything after the entries have been through the database and come back, and appending from two requests at once needs two real connections to be anything more than a hope.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.WalletTestDatabase
comment:
The PostgreSQL the integration tests run against.

A real one, and the same version {@code docker compose} uses, because the tests that need a database are about what the database itself does: the trigger that refuses to change the ledger and the constraints that refuse an impossible group of credits. Neither exists in an in-memory database, and a test of a rule that is not there proves nothing.

One container for the whole test run. Starting it costs a couple of seconds; starting one per test class would cost that every time.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.BalanceTest
comment: The balance US23 shows: the total, where it came from, and what dies when.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.CreditLotTest
comment: What a group of credits does and does not allow.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.LedgerChainTest
comment:
What the chain of hashes is for: noticing that the history was changed.

The database already refuses {@code UPDATE} and {@code DELETE} on the ledger. This is about what happens when the change did not go through the database's rules at all: a restored backup, or a superuser who dropped the trigger first.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.RefundPlanTest
comment: Where a refund puts the credits back.

methods.name: chain
methods.comment: Writes the movements down as the ledger would, one after the other.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.SpendingPlanTest
comment: The order credits are spent in, which is the rule booking depends on.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.WalletFixtures
comment:
Groups of credits for the tests of the rules, built around a clock that does not move.

Every rule in wallet is about time: what expires first, what has expired already, what never expires. Read from the real clock, none of them could be tested without waiting, so the tests decide what "now" is and the rules are given it.

methods.name: seedExpiredDaysAgo
methods.comment: A grant that died before now, still holding credits nobody spent.

methods.name: purchased
